summary: Crossing the Sea of Galilee, Jesus warns His disciples against the leaven of the Pharisees, and they think He is talking about the bread they forgot.
key_insight: Jesus does not explain the riddle at first. He makes the disciples count the leftover baskets from both feedings, “Twelve” and “Seven,” because the answer to their worry was in their own memory.
story: Jesus left the Pharisees, got into the boat again and set out for the other side. {Mk} The disciples had forgotten to take bread, and they had only one loaf with them in the boat. {Mk}

On the way Jesus charged them, “Take heed, beware of the leaven of the Pharisees and the leaven of Herod.” {Mk} Matthew records the warning as the leaven “of the Pharisees and the Sadducees.” {Mt} The disciples began reasoning among themselves, “It is because we have no bread.” {Mk}

Jesus knew what they were saying. “O you of little faith,” {Mt} He said, “Why do you reason because you have no bread? Do you not yet perceive nor understand? Is your heart still hardened? Having eyes, do you not see? And having ears, do you not hear? And do you not remember?” {Mk}

“When I broke the five loaves for the five thousand, how many baskets full of fragments did you take up?” They said to Him, “Twelve.” “Also, when I broke the seven for the four thousand, how many large baskets full of fragments did you take up?” And they said, “Seven.” {Mk}

So He said to them, “How is it you do not understand?” {Mk} He had not been speaking about bread at all. Then they understood that He was warning them against the doctrine of the Pharisees and Sadducees. {Mt}
differences: Matthew’s warning names “the Pharisees and the Sadducees”; Mark’s names “the Pharisees and the leaven of Herod.”
Only Mark mentions the one loaf in the boat and the questions about eyes, ears and a hardened heart.
Matthew records “O you of little faith”; Mark has the disciples answer aloud, “Twelve” and “Seven.”
Matthew ends with the disciples understanding that leaven meant “the doctrine of the Pharisees and Sadducees.” Mark ends with Jesus’ question, “How is it you do not understand?”

fit.question: Matthew’s warning names the Sadducees; Mark’s names Herod. Which did Jesus say?

points.label: All three
points.text: Pharisees and Sadducees had just come together to test Him (Matthew 16:1), and Herod’s supporters had earlier joined the Pharisees in plotting against Him (Mark 3:6). Jesus may well have named all three, and each writer records part of the warning.

points.label: One circle, two labels
points.text: The Sadducees and the Herodians both stood for holding power and keeping peace with Rome. Some think Matthew names this circle by its religious label and Mark by its political one.

fit.note: Both writers record the same warning against the outlook of Jesus’ opponents; the difference in names requires no error.
fit.short: Jesus may have named all three groups, or Matthew and Mark name one circle of opponents by its religious and political labels.

scene.label: Leaven
scene.text: Leaven was a lump of old fermented dough kept back and worked into the next batch. A little spread through the whole lump. Israel cleared it from every house at Passover (Exodus 12:15), and Scripture often uses it for a hidden influence that spreads (1 Corinthians 5:6).

scene.label: The leaven of Herod
scene.text: Herod Antipas ruled Galilee and Perea. He had beheaded John the Baptist, and he was curious about Jesus (Luke 9:9). His supporters, the Herodians, had already plotted with the Pharisees against Him (Mark 3:6).

scene.label: Eyes that do not see
scene.text: Jesus’ questions echo Jeremiah 5:21, which speaks of a people “who have eyes and see not, and who have ears and hear not.” After the first feeding, Mark had said of the disciples that “their heart was hardened” (Mark 6:52).

scene.label: Toward Bethsaida
scene.text: From the Magdala shore the boat crossed back to the northeast, toward Bethsaida, where Mark’s next scene takes place (Mark 8:22).

witnesses.matthew: Ends with understanding: the disciples grasp that leaven means teaching. Matthew repeatedly pairs the Pharisees and Sadducees in this chapter (16:1, 6, 11–12), presenting them as one front against Jesus.
witnesses.mark: Ends with a question instead of an answer: “How is it you do not understand?” Mark piles up Jesus’ questions, then tells of a blind man who sees only gradually (Mark 8:22–26), a picture of disciples who still see in part.

seeing.reveals: Jesus is patient with His disciples but does not leave them in their confusion. He presses them with questions, makes them count the baskets, and points them back to what His own hands have done.
seeing.living: The disciples worried about one missing loaf while sitting beside the One who had fed nine thousand men. When small anxieties crowd the mind, count the baskets: name what He has already done. And watch for the quiet influences, religious or worldly, that shape how you see Him.
seeing.ponder: If Jesus asked you to count the baskets, the times He has provided for you, what would you name, and how would that change today’s worry?

preaching.big_idea: Remembering what Jesus has done guards us against worry and against the leaven of unbelief.
preaching.watch_for: The words “understand” and “remember” drive the passage, and the hardest question comes last. Mark places this scene just before the blind man healed in two stages (8:22–26).
